newsitem.title: SPAIN: Headaches, nerves mix with smiles at NATO summit.
newsitem.headline: Headaches, nerves mix with smiles at NATO summit.

text.p: While NATO leaders made history on Tuesday by agreeing to expand the alliance to the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland, their landmark summit had its lighter side.

Alonso, youngest son of Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, could not resist a close-up peek at U.S. President Bill Clinton. Photographers caught the nine-year-old and a friend sneaking through the bushes at a joint news conference by the two leaders in the grounds of the prime minister's residence.

U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton slipped away from her husband and the spotlight to visit the ancient Spanish cathedral town of Toledo and do some souvenir shopping with her 17-year-old daughter Chelsea.
Onlookers applauded as Hillary chatted and laughed with local officials and gamely navigating the steep, cobbled alleyways with Chelsea.

French President Jacques Chirac also got a warm reception when he walked into his news conference and a cluster of Romanian journalists burst into applause. Other reporters looked on in bemusement or disapproval.
"That's the least I can expect," a delighted Chirac beamed. "I suspect that may be from your Romanian colleagues, whom I greet particularly warmly."

The Romanians were delighted at Chirac's hard-fought battle to win their country the prospect of admission to NATO in a second wave of enlargement after a 1999 review, after the United States blocked their entry in the first wave.

Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski, whose country did receive the coveted invitation, spent a tense afternoon waiting for the telephone call confirming the news from NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana.
He had invited journalists and promised interviews to record the moment, due shortly after noon, at a central Madrid hotel.

But it was not until just before 5 p.m. after a long afternoon with nervous Polish officials chain-smoking and pacing the hotel lobby, that the phone rang and a beaming, relieved Kwasniewski emerged to board his waiting limousine for the cross-town journey to the summit meeting.

Nothing quite ran to time at the high-tech conference centre close to Madrid airport. The sessions were extended while Chirac haggled for a better deal for countries not invited to join NATO's first wave of enlargement.

Even Solana was late. The 16 NATO leaders, lined up for a group photo session, started to fidget as they waited for the bearded secretary-general. The normally distinguished crowd burst into cheers and applause as the tardy Spaniard ran up.

The physical strain of the summit caused more than 100 people to seek care from the site medical services with journalists the biggest casualties as they got bumps, scrapes and headaches scrambling frantically after NATO delegates.
A security guard compared the stampede of photographers and television camera crews with Spain's famous bull-running festival, which by coincidence is taking place during the week of the summit.

"Watch out, here's the running of the bulls," he joked as the journalists raced through the hallways jockeying for a good position for Solana's historic statement. Several people have been gored in Pamplona this year.

In a new twist on NATO summit protests, a tiny group of Lithuanians demonstrated in favour of the military alliance. Wearing t-shirts that spelled out the name of the Baltic state, and waving green, red and yellow flags, 20 members of Lithuanian Youth for NATO urged allied leaders to support aspirations by Baltic states for full and early membership.

More traditionally, about a dozen anti-nuclear protesters from Belgium's For Mother Earth International and the British World Court Project, outnumbered three-to-one by police, held a press briefing outside a Spanish metro station dressed in nuclear safety suits adorned with sunflowers. They planned to summons NATO leaders for failing to abolish nuclear weapons.

With NATO delegations occupying every major hotel in Madrid, tourists faced machine guns and armoured cars just trying to get to their rooms. A middle-aged man from Lynn, Massachusetts, said it was only when a U.S. bodyguard recognised him from high school that he was allowed to enter his hotel while Clinton was there.
But he did not really mind and was thrilled to share buffet breakfast with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
